newsitem.title: USA: Intuit to set up online financial bazaar.
newsitem.headline: Intuit to set up online financial bazaar.

text.p: Intuit Inc. , maker of the best-selling Quicken personal finance software, plans to reshape itself into an online bazaar for financial services.
During the next two years, the Menlo Park, Calif., company will roll out several sites on the World Wide Web where people can buy insurance policies, get home mortgages or set up retirement plans.

Just like online booksellers and CD stores, Intuit would get a cut of every product sold through its site. But Intuit's line of work would be much more lucrative: the commission on a $500,000 life insurance policy is much bigger than the cut on a $10 paperback.
"We believe there's a huge business opportunity in providing the marketplace where buyers can meet sellers of financial services," Scott Cook, Intuit's chairman, said in a recent interview.
In fact, Cook is betting Intuit's future on the online business. Trouble is, no one knows how long it will take before people feel comfortable shopping for life insurance through the Web.

The automatic teller machine at the bank took 15 years to catch on. But Cook cannot wait that long. Intuit, like other consumer software companies, is facing slowing revenue growth because of collapsing software prices.
Banks and personal computer makers practically give away Intuit's flagship product, Quicken. And competitors are selling tax software, another big source of revenue for Intuit, for as little as $5.

The company last week told investors to expect revenue of $600 million to $620 million for the current fiscal year -- about $40 million shy of what Wall street expected -- because of its slowing software business.
Explosive growth from online financial services will not come too soon, investors said.

"The question is not if it will work, the question is when," said Liz Buyer, a money manager at T. Rowe Price, which owns about 1 million Intuit shares. "So it's difficult for investors to completely embrace the idea."
In recent quarters, online financial service revenue has been the fastest-growing segment of Intuit's business. But it has been minuscule -- about $3 million in the first quarter.
"We're doing stuff here that's revolutionary," Cook said. "That makes predictions harder."
Analysts agree that Intuit is indeed doing revolutionary stuff.

At Intuit's InsureMarket Web site (www.insuremarket.com), customers shopping for life insurance take two minutes to type in a general description of their health. Seconds later, they get quotes for policies from three competing insurance companies. No cryptic forms, no long-winded sales pitches. Three mouse-clicks later and the customer has a life insurance policy.
By year-end a handful of other insurance companies will be on the site, Cook said. Some time this year, Intuit also will offer car and home insurance.
Upcoming sites will sell home mortgages and retirement plans, Cook said.

Of course, it's relatively to enter the vending business on the Internet. Yahoo Inc., Microsoft Corp. and other companies with popular Web sites could easily set up similar pages. But Intuit has a huge lead because of the dominance of Quicken in the personal finance software market, analysts said.
Cook, a former product manager at Proctor & Gamble Co., also has lots of experience coaxing conservative banker types into online businesses, analysts said.
"If anybody is able to make a go of online commerce, it would be Intuit," said Steve Higgins, at Bear, Stearns & Co. in San Francisco.
Higgins, however, rates Intuit's stock only as "neutral." Bazaars are not set up over night, he said.
